study.title: John 12 Honor Jesus, increasing rejection and the hour of glorification
study.overview: John 12 shows, in increasing tension, the public honor given to Jesus and the opposition that intensifies against him. The anointing in Bethany reveals love and spiritual discernment; the triumphal entrance to Jerusalem fulfills Scripture and manifests Jesus as King, although the crowd understands it partially. The arrival of Greeks anticipates that their mission will attain beyond Israel, but Jesus responds by speaking of his hour: his death would be the way to fruitful, judge the world and attract people from all backgrounds. The chapter ends with a solemn appeal: to believe in the light while it is present, for rejecting the words of Jesus brings judgment on the last day.

outline.title: Unit in Bethany and Threat Against Lazarus
outline.explanation: Jesus goes to Bethany before the Passover and is served in a supper in his honor. Mary anoints Jesus" feet with an expensive perfume, in a gesture of devotion that fills the house with fragrance. Judas criticizes the action under the appearance of social concern, but the gospel reveals his corrupt motivation. Jesus interprets the anointing as preparation for his burial. Lazarus' presence leads many to believe, and the leaders even plan to kill Lazarus, because he became a living witness to the power of Jesus.

outline.title: Triumphal entry into Jerusalem and reaction of leaders
outline.explanation: The next day Jesus enters Jerusalem and the crowd receives him with branches and Messianic acclaims. When riding on a collear, he fulfills Scripture and presents himself as King in humility. The disciples understand only fully after the glorification of Jesus. Popular enthusiasm contrasts with the frustration of the Pharisees, who realize that their influence spreads more and more.

outline.title: The Greeks, the hour of Jesus and the call to walk in the light
outline.explanation: Some Greeks wish to see Jesus, a sign that his fame already surpasses the Jewish environment. Jesus responds by declaring that the time has come to be glorified, and explains his death with the figure of the grain of wheat that he must die to bear much fruit. He calls his servants to follow him, linking service, renunciation, and honor given by the Father. Then he speaks of his anguish and gives the will to the Father. The voice of heaven confirms his mission and announces the defeat of the prince of this world. Jesus declares that being raised from the earth, he will draw everyone to himself. Then he exhorts the crowd to walk in the light while he still has it, so as not to be taken by darkness.

outline.title: Unbelief, the glory of God, and the judgment of the word
outline.explanation: Even after so many signs, many do not believe, and John reads this resistance to the light of the testimony of Isaiah. Even among the chiefs there was those who believed, but the fear of exclusion and love of human glory prevented them from openly confessing faith. Jesus then summarizes his identity and mission: to believe in him is to believe in the Father who sent him; seeing him is to see the Sent. He reaffirms that he came as light to take people out of darkness and save the world. He who rejects his words is already under condemnation, for the very word of Jesus will judge him on the last day. All that he speaks proceeds from the commandment of the Father, which is presented as eternal life.

study.context: The chapter takes place in the days immediately before the Passover, when pilgrims ascend to Jerusalem for the feast. The scenario is of intense religious expectation and of great public visibility for Jesus. The notes highlight the sequence of the final events of Jesus" week and the increasing opposition of the religious authorities.
study.theology: John 12 unites revelation, cross, and judgment. Jesus is glorified not despite death, but through her: his death bears fruit, defeats the power of evil and draws people to him. The figure of light shows that the revelation of God in Christ is not neutral; before it, one responds with faith or hardening. The chapter also emphasizes the union between Jesus and the Father: seeing Jesus is to see the Envoy, to believe in him is to believe in the Father himself, and his words have eschatological authority. Human reaction reveals the heart: some worship, others use religion for self-interest, and many love social approval more than the glory of God.

scholarViews.insight: The hour of judgment begins when the light of Christ enters into darkness and unmasks evil; his work undoes the dominion of Satan.
The unbelief of many was in itself a shame, but also the fulfillment of what Isaiah had already announced.
The commandment received from the Father is presented as eternal life; therefore, all that Jesus speaks comes as a message of life.

questions: What in my devotion to Jesus looks like the gesture of Mary, and what resembles the criticism of Judas?
Have I followed the light of Christ with practical obedience, or just admired Jesus without surrendering to him?
Am I more afraid to lose people's approval than dishonor God's glory?
study.practice: Set up time to review your response to Jesus in three areas: worship, witness, and decision. Worship: offer Christ something Icaro, that is, time, resources or attention that you normally hold to you. Testimony: do not hide your faith for fear of rejection; publicly confess that Jesus is the Father's Envoy. Decision: Identify an area where you are deferring obedience and choose to act while there is still light. Apply also the principle of wheat grain: accept that some losses for love of Christ can become fruit for the Kingdom.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not detail all possible historical elements of the paschal context, and it was not necessary to use external information. There is also interpretative uncertainty in some points, such as the exact identity of the "Greeks" and the precise way of understanding the speech about the voice of the sky; therefore, they were presented only as possibilities in line with the notes, without affirmations beyond them.
